newsitem.title: USA: Fed to watch repo mkt for "special"-NY Fed Fisher.
newsitem.headline: Fed to watch repo mkt for "special"-NY Fed Fisher.

text.p: The Federal Reserve Bank of New York will carefully monitor repo market participants who attempt to create artifically tight trading conditions for specific issues, Peter Fisher, Manager of the System Open Market Account at the New York Fed, said on Tuesday.

"To put it bluntly, the surest way to subject yourself to heightened scrutiny by the New York Fed is to attempt to deliver to us large amounts of collateral that is trading deeply on special," Fisher told the Money Marketeers of New York University.

In the repurchase agreement market, an issue trades "on special" when demand commands a premium. Repo traders can push such premium higher by declining to make available issues that are already scarce.

"We (the New York Fed) refuse to accept collateral that is trading persistently on special and will instruct dealers to arrange a substitution should an issue, already submitted in a term operation, go on special," Fisher added.
Fisher also warned that "it is not the purpose of the New York Fed's market surveillance efforts to make the market safe for short sellers."
He pointed out that the hallmark of an efficient market is "when there is a healthy, competitive dynamic between the risks of holding long positions and the risks of holding short positions."
Fisher's remarks came as the New York Fed just published a paper by economist Frank Keane on the trading pattern for secondary-market issues in between Treasury auctions.

"Understanding this cycle...described in an article by Frank Keane...has been essential in our work on market surveillance because it gives us more appropriate benchmarks with which to compare repo rates," Fisher said.

The New York Fed senior official cited three criteria that would lead regulators to suspect an attempt to corner specific issues in the repo market: Holding a long position of more than half of an issue on special; representing more than one quarter of the turnover in a specific issue over days; and holding an issue that continuously trades within 50 basis points of the "fails rate", or a zero-to-50 point rate.
Fisher said meeting these criteria, or being involved in more than 50 percent of the turnover in a specific issue on special "will give rise to heightened concern on our part."
If it has "sufficient grounds" to suspect an attempt at cornering the market, the New York Fed will refer the case to the appropriate regulators, Fisher added.
Fisher also said Keane's work has shed light on "the critical role the repo market plays in the price discovery process in the cash market."
Such a role has led the repo market to "become an essential component of the market-making process in the cash market," Fisher added.
